query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to 300 mm in the HVAF-i7 process will enhance deposition efficiency and yield thicker FeCoNiCrAl coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with the standard 15–45 μm size distribution applied in HVAF-i7 deposition.
generation.intervention: Adjust the nozzle-to-substrate distance to a fixed value of 300 mm.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed within confined geometries (internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under typical HVAF-i7 conditions with otherwise unaltered gas and feedstock parameters.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced spray distance minimizes particle deceleration and oxidation while maximizing kinetic energy on impact.
generation.mechanism: A shorter, optimized spray distance prevents significant loss of particle momentum and limits the exposure time to ambient oxygen, thus improving splat integrity and encouraging thicker, denser bonding deposits.
generation.predicted_outcome: An approximate 15–25% increase in coating thickness relative to the baseline HVAF-i7 deposition (with a longer or non-optimized distance) without compromising the as-sprayed oxidation level or adhesion.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 deposited coatings at a non-optimized nozzle distance leading to lower than desired thickness.
generation.boundary: The optimum distance must balance particle kinetic energy with the risk of increased substrate heating or geometric restrictions in small diameters; too short a distance could induce impact defects.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal 300 mm distance may require fine-tuning based on specific torch configurations and substrate geometries; the improvement magnitude may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit coatings using the HVAF-i7 system at various nozzle-to-substrate distances (e.g., 250 mm, 300 mm, 350 mm) on identical substrates with a 15–45 μm feedstock. Compare thickness, microstructure, and oxidation levels.
measurements: Porosity and oxidation state via EDS analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings deposited at 300 mm do not show a statistically significant improvement in thickness (≥15% thicker) and quality compared to those at other distances, or if signs of degradation (e.g., increased oxidation) appear, then the hypothesis is falsified.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy powder deposited via HVOF
papers.approach: Varying spray distance to study the effects of particle kinetic energy and in‐flight oxidation on coating characteristics
papers.findings: Coatings sprayed from longer distances exhibited lower particle kinetic energy, increased in-flight oxidation and porosity, and reduced microhardness. Optimal deposition efficiency was linked to higher particle velocity, as inferred from the variation in spray distance.
papers.mechanism: Higher particle velocity gives particles greater momentum to impact and adhere, leading to denser and thicker coatings. In contrast, longer spraying distances allow extended exposure to oxygen, which causes oxidation and increased porosity that reduce effective deposition efficiency.

papers.title: Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy coatings produced by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS)
papers.approach: Plasma spraying followed by high‐temperature oxidation tests to evaluate phase transformations and coating integrity
papers.findings: The coatings developed a lamellar structure with a controlled oxide layer (such as Al2O3), and the oxidation behavior was strongly affected by the spray thermal history. The coatings maintained good adhesion with minor porosity and demonstrated phase stability across a range of temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Selective oxidation (mainly of aluminum) leads to the formation of protective oxide scales that stabilize the coating structure. The spray process parameters govern the extent of oxidation and phase transformation, influencing coating performance.

papers.title: Comparative Study on the Thermal Performance of Cr-CrₓO_y and YSZ-CoNiCrAlY Coatings Exposed at 900 °C.
papers.system: Conventional MCrAlY bond coats deposited via HVOF
papers.approach: Optimizing spray parameters, particularly focusing on particle velocity and nozzle-to-substrate distance (notably 300 and 350 mm), to improve deposition efficiency and coating adhesion
papers.findings: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was achieved with higher particle velocities and specifically optimized nozzle distances, which also improved mechanical bonding and reduced the formation of interlamellar defects.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced kinetic energy improves the in-flight melting and impact dynamics of the particles, leading to better splat formation and lower porosity. This increases coating thickness while maintaining adhesion.

papers.title: Growth Mechanisms and the Effects of Deposition Parameters on the Structure and Properties of High Entropy Film by Magnetron Sputtering.
papers.system: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy films produced by magnetron sputtering
papers.approach: Systematic variation of deposition parameters (substrate temperature, deposition power, and target configuration) to assess their effects on film microstructure and thickness
papers.findings: Deposition conditions played a critical role in determining the microstructure, which featured columnar grains and homogeneity. Film thickness and phase are strongly controlled by the sputtering parameters.
papers.mechanism: By adjusting deposition energy and substrate positioning, the coating density and thickness can be optimized, suggesting that similar kinetic principles also apply in thermal spray processes.

established: A narrow feedstock size (15–45 μm) provides high-quality, dense coatings under HVAF-M3 processing.
Optimal deposition efficiency in MCrAlY systems has been achieved by increasing particle velocity and adjusting spray distances (300–350 mm).
Uniform coating quality with low as-sprayed oxidation is closely tied to controlling in-flight oxidation and particle thermal history.

approaches_tried.outcome: Produced high-quality, adherent coatings with the correct microstructure and minimal oxidation; resulted in sufficient thickness in that system.

approaches_tried.approach: HVAF-i7 deposition with the same 15–45 μm feedstock
approaches_tried.outcome: Coating quality remained acceptable but the overall coating thickness was inadequate.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing spray parameters (particle velocity and nozzle distance at 300–350 mm) in conventional MCrAlY systems
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved a slight gain in deposition efficiency and improved adhesion in bond coat applications.

mechanisms: Enhanced particle velocity increases kinetic energy, which improves in-flight melting and bonding, leading to thicker deposits.
Spray distance directly affects particle temperature and oxidation exposure: insufficient energy leads to thinner coatings and higher porosity.
Controlled in-flight oxidation promotes formation of protective oxide scales that are beneficial for high-temperature performance without compromising deposition efficiency.
disagreements: There is some divergence on how feedstock size and spray distance interplay between different torch systems (HVAF-M3 versus HVAF-i7).
The beneficial aspects of slight in-flight oxidation (for tribological performance) versus its detrimental impact on microhardness and thickness are still debated.
open_questions: Will increasing the particle velocity in the HVAF-i7 system overcome the thickness limitation while preserving coating integrity and minimal oxidation?

What are the optimal spray conditions (nozzle configuration, fuel/oxygen ratios, spray distance) for achieving thick, adherent coatings in restricted geometries (internal diameters as small as 120 mm)?
How do differences in torch design between HVAF-M3 and HVAF-i7 specifically affect the energy transfer and deposition efficiency for FeCoNiCrAl alloys?
opportunities: A concrete intervention opportunity is to adjust (increase) the particle velocity in the HVAF-i7 torch—either by modifying fuel/oxygen ratios or optimizing nozzle design—to enhance the kinetic energy of the 15–45 μm feedstock particles.
Investigate whether adopting a spray distance similar to that found optimal for conventional MCrAlY bond coats (300–350 mm) in the HVAF-i7 context can recover the lost deposition thickness.
Combine increased particle velocity with controlled in-flight oxidation to target thicker, high-quality coatings for demanding internal geometries.

Future work could design a controlled experiment comparing standard HVAF-i7 processing with the proposed intervention to directly measure coating thickness, microstructure, and oxidation levels under identical deposition and high-temperature service conditions.

directions.direction: Increase the in-flight particle kinetic energy by raising the particle velocity through optimizing the fuel/oxygen ratio in the HVAF-i7 torch.
directions.assessment: This direction directly addresses the thickness limitation by imparting higher momentum to the particles, enhancing splat formation and deposition efficiency. It is supported by studies on conventional MCrAlY systems (e.g., record IDs PMC8541463::web::003 and PMC8541463::web::022) and is technically feasible with careful control of combustion parameters.

directions.direction: Optimize the nozzle‐to‐substrate distance in the HVAF-i7 system to around 300–350 mm.
directions.assessment: By setting the spray distance similar to that used in conventional MCrAlY studies, the particles retain higher kinetic energy and reduced in-flight oxidation. This modification is directly linked to improved deposition efficiency, as evidenced by prior work and is practical for maintaining coating integrity in confined geometries.

directions.direction: Modify the nozzle design (e.g., employing a convergent-divergent nozzle) to further accelerate the powder particles.
directions.assessment: A redesigned nozzle geometry can focus and accelerate the particle stream, increasing the particles’ impact energy. While this approach is more involved in terms of hardware modification, it targets the thickness limitation directly by increasing deposition efficiency while still remaining within the expected physics of thermal spray processes.

directions.direction: Introduce a pulsed gas flow synchronized with particle injection to create temporal bursts of higher particle velocity.
directions.assessment: This approach uses a dynamic gas flow control to temporarily boost particle acceleration without changing the feedstock. The transient increase in kinetic energy could enhance splat formation and deposition rate. Although less explored, the physics is supported by analogous pulsed acceleration methods; feasibility and process stability require careful validation.

directions.direction: Preheat the substrate to adjust the thermal gradient during deposition.
directions.assessment: While preheating can influence coating adhesion and splat spreading, its direct impact on overall deposit thickness is less clear compared to interventions targeting particle dynamics. It may contribute indirectly to coating integrity but does not primarily address the deposition thickness limitation.

candidates.hypothesis: Increasing the HVAF-i7 particle velocity by optimizing the fuel/oxygen ratio will overcome the thickness limitation of FeCoNiCrAl coatings.
candidates.intervention: Increase the fuel/oxygen ratio by approximately 10–15% to boost the combustion intensity thereby raising the particle velocity during in-flight flight.

candidates.hypothesis: Optimizing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to 300 mm in the HVAF-i7 process will enhance deposition efficiency and yield thicker FeCoNiCrAl coatings.

candidates.hypothesis: Adopting a modified convergent-divergent nozzle design in the HVAF-i7 torch to focus and accelerate particles will produce thicker FeCoNiCrAl coatings.
candidates.intervention: Replace the standard nozzle with a convergent-divergent nozzle configuration designed to further accelerate and focus the particle stream.

candidates.hypothesis: Implementing a pulsed gas flow synchronized with the particle injection in the HVAF-i7 process will transiently boost particle velocity and lead to thicker FeCoNiCrAl coatings.
candidates.intervention: Introduce a pulsed gas flow system that produces periodic bursts of higher gas velocity synchronized with powder injection.

major_issues: Lack of prior demonstrations of pulsed gas flow in HVAF complicates confidence in the mechanism.
Potential technical complexities in synchronizing pulses with powder injection could lead to unstable spray conditions.
minor_issues: Unclear whether pulsing can be effectively tuned to avoid excessive oxidation or coating defects.
fixes: Provide preliminary experimental or modeling data on pulsed flow feasibility for HVAF.
Detail how pulse frequency and duration would be optimized and controlled in real time.
evidence_needs: Published case studies (if any) on pulsed gas flow in thermal spray processes for validation.
Data on spray plume stability and deposit microstructure when subjected to pulsed flow.
